exam: A patient presents with bloody diarrhea and mild abdominal pain; stool microscopy is negative. What is your next diagnostic step and why? — Order an antigen detection ELISA because microscopy can miss low‑level infection and ELISA has higher sensitivity.

Explain how cysteine proteases contribute to the clinical picture of amoebic dysentery. — They degrade collagen and inactivate complement, leading to deep ulceration with little inflammation and rapid blood loss.

A 30‑year‑old farmer from a low‑resource hospital has a right‑upper‑quadrant mass and fever; ultrasound shows a single hypoechoic lesion. What is the most likely diagnosis and the first‑line therapy? — Amoebic liver abscess; start metronidazole followed by a luminal agent.
Why is drainage of an amoebic liver abscess not routinely performed? — Most respond to metronidazole; drainage is reserved for large (>5 cm), ruptured, or non‑responding lesions.

Differentiate Entamoeba histolytica from Entamoeba dispar in a clinical setting. — E. dispar is non‑invasive and does not cause dysentery; only E. histolytica produces cysteine proteases that degrade ECM.

A patient on metronidazole develops peripheral neuropathy. What alternative tissue‑active drug can be used and why is it less preferred? — Tinidazole is an alternative but is less available and more costly in low‑resource settings.
How does HIV infection modify the presentation of amoebiasis? — Higher risk of severe colitis and multiple liver abscesses due to impaired immunity.

What laboratory finding may be falsely normal in severe amoebic colitis and why? — White blood cell count may be normal because neutrophils are killed by amoebapores, masking the inflammatory response.
ai.title: Entamoeba histolytica Extracellular Matrix Degradation
ai.subject: Microbiology & immunology
ai.summary: Entamoeba histolytica uses cysteine proteases and amoebapores to break down extracellular matrix, facilitating intestinal invasion and liver abscess formation. Understanding this mechanism guides diagnosis and management in low‑resource settings.

b: Transmission: fecal‑oral via cysts in contaminated water/food
sections.p: Entamoeba histolytica is a protozoan parasite causing amoebic dysentery and extra‑intestinal disease, especially liver abscesses. Its virulence hinges on enzymes that degrade host extracellular matrix (ECM).

b: Cysteine proteases (e.g., CP1, CP2) degrade collagen, laminin, fibronectin
Amoebapores form pores in host cell membranes, causing lysis
sections.p: Trophozoites are motile, have a single nucleus with a central karyosome, and possess surface lectins for adherence.

b: Cysts survive in moist environments for weeks
sections.p: Ingested cysts excyst in the small intestine; trophozoites colonize the colon, may invade mucosa, and can enter the portal circulation to reach the liver.

b: Intestinal: bloody diarrhea, abdominal cramps, mucus
Extra‑intestinal: right‑upper‑quadrant pain, fever, tender hepatomegaly
sections.p: Clinical spectrum ranges from mild colitis to fulminant dysentery and hepatic abscesses.

t.b: Detects trophozoites or cysts; confirms intestinal infection – may miss low‑grade disease
Answers presence of E. histolytica antigen; high sensitivity, useful when microscopy unavailable
Identifies hypoechoic lesions; distinguishes abscess from other masses when CT not accessible
Positive in most hepatic abscesses; negative early infection

b: Metronidazole (tissue‑active) – kills trophozoites and hepatic abscess organisms
Luminal agent (paromomycin or iodoquinol) – eliminates cysts in the intestine
Drainage only if abscess >5 cm, fails to respond, or causes rupture risk
sections.p: Eradicate trophozoites, then address abscess if present.

b: Cysteine proteases → collagen breakdown → deep ulceration with minimal inflammation
Amoebapores → rapid cell lysis → bloody stools
Liver abscess often without peritoneal signs because ECM degradation limits spread
sections.p: Focus on the link between ECM‑degrading enzymes and the clinical picture.

whenToSeekHelp: Severe dehydration, shock, or persistent high fever
Signs of perforation: sudden severe abdominal pain, guarding, rigidity
Large (>5 cm) liver abscess with risk of rupture
